title: Is It an Engagement Problem, or a Decision Problem?

Two products, eight years apart, where I read the same situation wrong. Abhishek Anand 7 min read · Sep 22, 2026 -- Listen Share We spent about three months building a research tool for fantasy cricket. Five numbers per player, nothing exotic. Recent form over the last five matches, record against the team playing tonight, record at that ground, what the player does in specific phases of the game, and a comparison screen for when you are stuck between two picks. The users we cared most about liked it. They used it properly, the way you would use a spreadsheet before putting money on something. And then a number of them closed our app and built their teams on Dream11. This was 2021, at BalleBaazi. We were the challenger. Dream11 had the users and the prize money and could copy anything clever we shipped inside a quarter. The first suggestion in the room was to put the tool behind a contest entry, which is a fair thing to suggest. We had paid for the data, built the screens, and were now running a free research desk for the market leader’s customers. Somebody was always going to say it. Nobody said anything intelligent in that meeting, me included. That took months. (If you have never touched fantasy sports: you pick a squad of real players before a match, name one of them captain for double points, and score on what they actually do on the field. It is forecasting with a game skin on it.) Why we built the thing in the first place Our matches fell into rough tiers. India games and World Cups, where every user knew every player. Leagues like the Big Bash, where recognition got thin. Domestic cricket, where most people were guessing. Participation tracked those tiers almost exactly, and since marquee matches are a small slice of a cricket calendar, the thin part was most of the year. Plot that and it looks like an engagement problem. Engagement problems have a standard response. More contests, bigger pools, notifications, a stats tab with more stats in it. What stopped us was something fairly dumb. Every cricket statistic a user could want was already free on the internet and they were not using it. Our users had more data within reach than a professional analyst had twenty years earlier, and they were still sitting matches out. Whatever was short, it was not information. I had seen this before and handled it worse From 2015 I owned the mock-test category for state-level government exams at OnlineTyari. Our users were aspirants in Tier-2 and Tier-3 towns, studying on mobile data that dropped without warning, mostly with no coaching available to them, and careful with money in a way that is hard to convey if you have not sold to that user. A test series was a considered purchase made by someone who could not afford a second mistake. We had over 500,000 questions. On paper that is an asset. In practice a student finished a mock test, saw a score, and had no idea what to do with the rest of their week. The obvious move was more content, better content, more tests. Content is the engagement lever in education and everyone in the category was pulling it. It took me a long time to see that a student sitting in front of 500,000 questions has the same problem as a fantasy user sitting in front of the entire internet. What we built At OnlineTyari, two projects that nobody would have called growth work. The tag tree came first. A taxonomy already existed; I made it deeper and made it operational, so every question carried subject, chapter, topic, sub-topic, difficulty and concept depth. Once the tagging was that dense, a wrong answer located the weakness instead of just docking a mark. A rule-based, priority-ordered, difficulty-aware layer then pointed at the question bank or eBook that closed that particular gap. Then offline mock tests. A three-hour paper on a connection that cuts out is a wasted Sunday, and for a user whose whole reason to practise is rehearsing exam temperament, worse than nothing. Download, attempt offline, sync when the network returns, analysis after sync. The first two tests in every series were free. We were not discounting anything. We wanted a student to watch the diagnosis work on their own weak spots before we asked them for money, because in that market nobody was going to take our word for it. At BalleBaazi the constraint showed up early. Computing lifetime statistics across every player, venue and matchup was past what our data infrastructure could do, and engineering said so before we had got far. We cut it and shipped last-five-match form from internal data, with a third-party feed for the deeper slices. The cut made the product better. For a decision about tonight, what a player averaged in 2014 is trivia. We also turned down three things people asked for. Predicted picks, an auto-team builder, and a confidence score attached to each player. The tool was there to inform the pick and then get out of the way. Whether that was principle or squeamishness I am still not completely sure, but I would hold the line again, and it matters more now than it did in 2021, because a good deal of what is shipping this year walks straight across it. The numbers, and what they do not cover In my category at OnlineTyari, monthly mock-test sales went from under 10,000 to 25,000-plus, with roughly a 30% lift in the first month after the changes.
